ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Josephine Baker Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Establishing care three weeks after a heart attack and stent, with breathlessness on exertion and tiredness: examination, ECG, laboratory tests, medicines, mood screening, cardiac rehabilitation and the chest-pain action plan. Concerns: She wants to return to the stage and to have the strength to care for her children; She is afraid of another heart attack and of what would happen to her family; Debts and lost income make every cost a worry. [S]

tr.td: Coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention in the hospital for a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction: 90% stenosis of the mid right coronary artery treated with one drug-eluting stent; mild disease elsewhere. Performed at a regional hospital before she established care
Twelve-lead electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm at 64 per minute, small Q waves in II, III and aVF from the recent inferior infarction, no acute ST change, normal QT
Outpatient cardiac rehabilitation, phase 2: 36 sessions over twelve weeks with exercise training, nutrition, stress management and psychological support; all sessions completed

Transthoracic echocardiography: ejection fraction 52%, hypokinesis of the basal and mid inferior wall, normal right ventricle, no thrombus, normal valves, normal estimated filling pressures, no pericardial effusion

Symptom-limited exercise treadmill test on her usual medicines (Bruce protocol): 9 minutes, about 10 METs, peak heart rate 132 per minute on metoprolol, normal blood pressure response (124/76 to 172/80), no angina, no ischemic ST change, no arrhythmia
Advance care planning conversation, about 20 minutes, with her consent

text.paragraph: Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Long, grave illness in Casablanca after the loss of a pregnancy: in bed in hospital from June 1941 to December 1942, with five operations, reportedly including an emergency hysterectomy, and peritonitis and septicemia (details from one secondary source; stillbirth or miscarriage disputed)
Heart attack in March 1969, on the day of her eviction from Les Milandes, with admission to hospital in Périgueux; described as a new heart attack, with any earlier one undated in the sources read

list.item: Entertainer, singer and dancer for more than forty years, in Paris and on tours around the world; has stopped performing while she recovers and wants to return to the stage [S]
Veteran of the wartime Resistance, decorated for intelligence work, and a civil rights activist who has spoken against segregation all her life [S]
Mother of twelve adopted children, some still at school; the family recently lost the home and estate where she raised them, and now lives in a rented house [S]
Finances: large debts from the estate; income only from performing, which has stopped since the heart attack; she is anxious about the cost of medicines and of the children's needs [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: rarely, a glass of champagne on occasion. No drug use [S]
Diet: irregular meals around rehearsals and travel, often late at night; enjoys cooking for her family; little salt added [S]

Says she waited until the morning to go to hospital, thinking the pressure in her chest was the strain of the eviction; asks that her account of her body be taken seriously and that she be told plainly what each medicine is for [S]

tr.td: Establishing care three weeks after a heart attack and stent, with breathlessness on exertion and tiredness: examination, ECG, laboratory tests, medicines, mood screening, cardiac rehabilitation and the chest-pain action plan
Two-week review: echocardiogram, cardiology consultation the same day, the cause of the breathlessness and the antiplatelet plan
Four-week review after the change to clopidogrel: breathlessness, blood pressure, potassium and kidney function, and cardiac rehabilitation
Twelve-week review: exercise test, lipids, mood, and the return to performing
Seven-month review: antiplatelet plan to twelve months, blood pressure, kidney function, angina status and plans for the year
Same-day sick visit for a nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Respectful, trauma-informed shared decisions: take her account of her symptoms seriously, explain each medicine and its reason plainly, write the plan down, and check costs with her before prescribing

Cardiology consultation on the day of the two-week visit, with an echocardiogram, to find the cause of the breathlessness, review the antiplatelet choice and the other medicines, and advise on rehabilitation and a return to the stage
Dual antiplatelet therapy, aspirin 81 mg with a P2Y12 inhibitor, for twelve months from the heart attack, never stopped without speaking to cardiology; then aspirin alone
Atorvastatin 80 mg daily; lipid panel four to eight weeks after the start; goal LDL below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall; lipoprotein(a) measured once

Metoprolol succinate for at least the first year after the heart attack; lisinopril for high blood pressure, with home readings and a target below 130/80 mmHg; potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after any dose change

Enroll in a 36-session outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program, starting within two weeks, with exercise training, nutrition, stress management and psychological support; the clinic will call her if she misses sessions
Depression after a heart attack: PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 today, repeat PHQ-9 at about twelve weeks, the rehabilitation program's psychologist, and a lower threshold for treatment if symptoms rise

Chest-pain action plan: nitroglycerin under the tongue, and 911 if pain is not better five minutes after the first tablet; warning symptoms in women, such as breathlessness, unusual tiredness, nausea or jaw, back or arm discomfort, explained
Costs: generic medicines in 90-day fills, the clinic social worker for debt advice and help with medicine costs, and rehabilitation sessions at times that fit her family
Women's cardiovascular risk: record the hysterectomy of her thirties and a possible early menopause as a risk-enhancing factor; hormone therapy is not used to prevent heart disease
Change ticagrelor to clopidogrel for ticagrelor-related breathlessness: 600 mg loading dose 24 hours after the last ticagrelor, then 75 mg daily, without a gap in antiplatelet cover
Raise lisinopril to 10 mg daily for blood pressure above target, with potassium and creatinine one to two weeks later
Laboratory tests drawn at the rehabilitation center on session days, so that no check needs a separate trip

Nosebleed plan on dual antiplatelet therapy: firm pressure on the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes, saline spray and a humidifier; do not stop aspirin or clopidogrel; come in if bleeding lasts more than 30 minutes
Graded return to the stage: rehearsals at the effort reached in rehabilitation, then full performances, with rest between shows, water, and nitroglycerin in the dressing room
Twelve months of dual antiplatelet therapy from the heart attack without interruption
Seven months completed without a missed dose; changed from ticagrelor to clopidogrel without a gap
LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall
Complete cardiac rehabilitation and return to performing
Exercise test to about 10 METs without ischemia; graded return to rehearsals agreed
Mood: PHQ-9 below 5 by twelve weeks

list.item: Independent in all daily activities; breathless after one flight of stairs or ten minutes of brisk walking, which before the heart attack never limited her; has not danced since [S]
Alert, warm and direct; worried about her family and her debts, and grieving the loss of her home; sleeps poorly; PHQ-9 score 7 with no thoughts of self-harm [S]
